blocks.prompt: The Bird That Eats Its Own Pink
blocks.text: A flamingo is not born pink. It hatches out of its egg soft and gray. Its beak is straight, not curved. The chick grows up on a nest made of mud, and its mom and dad feed it. Then the chick starts to find food for itself. It eats tiny shrimp and tiny plants from the water. Those foods are full of pink. Little by little, the gray feathers drop out and new pink feathers grow in. It takes about two years. A flamingo has to eat its way to pink.

blocks.prompt: How a Bird Eats Its Way to Pink
blocks.text: A flamingo chick hatches gray. Its beak is straight and its legs are wobbly. Nothing about it looks pink. Two years later, the same bird glows like a sunset. It did not change by magic. It ate its way there. Flamingos feed on tiny algae and small shrimp that live in salty water. Those tiny things are packed with colors called carotenoids, the same family of colors that makes carrots orange. When a flamingo eats them, its body breaks the colors apart and tucks them into its growing feathers, its skin, and even its beak. The more it eats, the pinker it gets. Flamingo parents feed their chick a rich pink milk that they make inside their own bodies. Feeding a chick costs so much color that the parents can turn pale while their baby grows. You can see the proof in a zoo. If keepers feed flamingos plain food with no carotenoids in it, the birds slowly fade to a dull white. Give the color back, and the pink comes back too. So a flamingo is not painted. It is built out of its dinner.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: In a flamingo, the upper jaw moves, not the lower one
Lamellae: comb-like plates that strain the water
The tongue pumps about four times a second
It filters its food the way a blue whale does

blocks.prompt: The Upside-Down Eater
blocks.text: Watch a flamingo eat and something looks wrong. The bird lowers its head into the water and turns it over, so the top of its beak is on the bottom. That is not clumsiness. That is the design. Most birds have a fixed upper jaw and a hinged lower one. Flamingos flipped the arrangement. Their lower jaw is the heavy, fixed part, and the upper jaw swings. Held upside down in the water, the beak works exactly the way a beak should. It is the bird that is turned over, not the tool. Inside the beak sit rows of tiny comb-like plates called lamellae. The flamingo's thick tongue pumps back and forth about four times a second, sucking muddy water in through the front of the beak and pushing it out the sides. The water leaves. The food stays behind: single-celled algae, small shrimp, and specks of shellfish too small to see. A flamingo is a filter with legs. There is a cost. A filter only works if there is something to filter, so flamingos gather where the water is thick with life: shallow salt lakes and lagoons that most birds avoid because the water is too salty, too alkaline, or too hot. The flamingo does not put up with those lakes by accident. It has them almost to itself. If the filtering reminds you of something else, it should. A blue whale feeds by pushing seawater through baleen plates and swallowing what is trapped. A flamingo weighs less than a large dog, and a blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, yet they solved the same problem the same way. Neither one inherited the idea from the other. Nature simply found a good answer twice.

blocks.prompt: The Lake That Only Flamingos Can Use
blocks.text: Lake Natron lies in northern Tanzania, at the foot of a mountain that erupts a strange pale lava loaded with sodium. Rain washes those salts down into the shallow basin, and because no river flows out again, they stay and concentrate. The water is alkaline enough to sting the skin and eyes of most animals that wade into it, and in the dry season parts of it climb past forty degrees Celsius. It is one of the least welcoming bodies of water on the continent. It is also the single most important nursery for lesser flamingos on Earth. Roughly three quarters of the world's lesser flamingos hatch there. The logic is cold and simple. Harshness is protection. Predators that would happily eat an egg do not cross caustic water, so the mud islands out in the middle of Natron are the safest cradles in Africa. Flamingos pay the entry fee with their bodies. Their long legs are wrapped in tough scales the water cannot easily damage, and glands near their eyes strain salt out of their blood and drip it away through their nostrils. What poisons other birds is merely their commute. The lake pays them back in food. Alkaline water suits a blue-green algae called Arthrospira, which blooms across Natron in enormous quantities and stains the surface deep red when you see it from the air. Lesser flamingos carry the finest filters of any flamingo, fine enough to strain out single cells. Nobody else at the lake can reach that food. Nobody else wants to try. Once the chicks hatch, thousands of them are herded into one gray crowd called a creche, watched over by a handful of adults while both parents fly off to feed. Then a parent returns to a crowd of thousands of nearly identical chicks and finds its own by calling. The chick answers. Out of that wall of noise, two birds pick out one voice each. The strategy has a weakness, and it is the same weakness that comes with putting everything in one place. Plans to build a soda ash plant on Natron have surfaced more than once. Nothing has been built. But a species that breeds almost nowhere else has no second lake to move to.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Phoenicopteridae: six living species
The backward joint is an ankle, not a knee
Chang and Ting, 2017: the one-legged stance costs almost no muscle

Mirandornithes means the miraculous birds

blocks.prompt: Everything You Know About the Flamingo Is a Little Bit Wrong
blocks.text: Everyone knows what a flamingo looks like, and almost everyone gets it wrong. Start with the leg. The joint halfway up a flamingo's leg bends backward, which looks like a knee installed the wrong way around. It is not a knee. It is an ankle. The flamingo's real knee sits high against its body, hidden under feathers, and it bends forward exactly like yours. What we are calling a shin is a foot. A flamingo, like every bird, walks permanently on tiptoe. Then there is the pose. A flamingo can stand on one leg for hours, sleeping, in wind, without visibly working at it. For a long time the standard explanation was heat: a bird standing in cold water bleeds warmth through its legs, so tucking one up halves the loss. That explanation is probably part of the truth. Flamingos do stand on one leg more often in cool water than in warm. But in 2017 two researchers, Young-Hui Chang and Lena Ting, tested something stranger. They took the body of a flamingo that had died at a zoo and stood it on one leg. It held the pose. A dead bird, with no muscles working at all, balanced. The joints, once stacked in the right position, lock under the animal's own weight. In living birds, sway actually drops as the flamingo dozes off, which is the opposite of what a difficult balancing act would do. Standing on one leg costs a flamingo almost nothing. It is resting in the cheapest position available to it. Now the family tree, which is where the flamingo becomes genuinely disorienting. For a century, biologists filed flamingos next to storks, or next to ducks, or next to herons, depending on which feature they weighted most. Long legs suggested storks. A filtering bill suggested ducks. Nobody could settle it, because a flamingo is a mosaic of borrowed-looking parts. Genetics settled it, and the answer was nobody's guess. The flamingo's closest living relatives are grebes: small, dumpy, short-legged diving birds that spend their lives low in freshwater ponds and can barely walk on land. Nothing about a grebe looks like a flamingo. Yet the DNA is unambiguous, and the two groups now share a branch with a name that admits the surprise: Mirandornithes, the miraculous birds. Whatever their common ancestor was, one line of its descendants went tall and pink and salt-tolerant, and the other went small and gray and underwater. That is the real lesson of the flamingo, and it is not about the pink. Looks lie. The leg that looks broken is built correctly. The pose that looks difficult is the easy one. The bird that looks like a stork is a cousin of something you would never pick out of a pond. Every one of those errors came from trusting appearance and stopping there. The flamingo has been standing in plain view the whole time, and we still had to test a body, sequence a genome, and measure the sway to work out what we were looking at.
